title: Constant-Time Map for Huge Numeric Keys
statement:
Objects in a system are identified by an `OBJ_ID` that is a very long decimal number. It is far too long for any primitive integer type, so it is given as a string of digits. Design a key-value store keyed by such IDs that supports three operations:

- `insert key value`: store `value` under `key`, replacing the old value if the key already exists. Print `1` if the key was new and `0` if an existing key was overwritten.
- `get key`: print the value stored under `key`, or `-1` if the key is absent.
- `delete key`: remove the key. Print `1` if it was present and `0` otherwise.

Keys are compared as exact digit strings, so leading zeros matter (`007` and `7` are different keys), and a key that is a prefix of another is a different key: deleting `12` must not affect `123`. All values are non-negative integers.

The operations are processed in the given order and every operation prints one line. The intended solution gives every operation a cost that depends only on the length `L` of the key and never on how many keys are stored, even in the worst case.

**Follow-up:** The interviewer asked for worst-case constant-time operations (in terms of the number of keys) and ruled out a standard hash map such as `unordered_map`, because adversarial keys can make its buckets degenerate to `O(n)`. Be ready to explain why a trie over the digits gives that guarantee, what it costs in memory, and how to free nodes on delete.
inputFormat: The first line contains the number of operations `q`. Each of the next `q` lines is one of `insert key value`, `get key` or `delete key`.
outputFormat: Print `q` lines, one per operation, containing the result of that operation as described above.
constraints: Each key is a string of 1 to 50 decimal digits (it may start with `0`)

examples.explanation: Both inserts add new keys (1, 1). The long key holds 5. `123` is only a prefix of stored keys, not a key itself, so `get` gives -1. Deleting `12345` succeeds (1), a later `get` gives -1. Re-inserting the long key overwrites it (0), and `get` then returns 9.
`007`, `7` and `07` are three different keys. `007` holds 1. Deleting `07` finds nothing (0), and `7` is untouched with value 2.

hints: A key does not have to be converted to a number. You can walk through it one digit at a time.
Build a trie with 10 children per node. Each node also remembers whether a key ends there and, if so, its value.
For delete, unmark the end node and then walk back up removing nodes that have no children and no stored key, so a deleted key never disturbs longer keys that share its prefix.
